Fasten verändert vorübergehend die Verfü: Fasting temporarily changes the availability of energy and nutrients. This can involve interesting biological adaptations – how strongly they occur varies between people, and the science is not yet conclusive in every area.
Autophagie ist ein körpereigener Prozess: Autophagy is the body's cellular recycling process: cells break down and reuse damaged or no-longer-needed components. Nutrient scarcity can stimulate this process in cell and animal models. It has not yet been firmly established whether a single 16–18-hour fast measurably increases autophagy in humans.
Mitophagie bezeichnet den gezielten Abba: Mitophagy is the selective removal of damaged or poorly functioning mitochondria. It is a specialised form of autophagy and helps maintain cellular quality control. However, it has not been shown that a weekly fasting window reliably increases this process in humans.
Während einer Essenspause sinkt der Insu: During a fasting window, insulin levels generally fall temporarily and the body increasingly draws on stored energy. Regular fasting patterns may improve body weight and some metabolic markers in certain people. Outcomes also depend on overall diet, energy balance and the fasting schedule.
Manche Menschen berichten während des Fa: Some people report feeling mentally clear or more mindful about meals while fasting. This is subjective and not universal: others experience hunger, fatigue or difficulty concentrating. Research has not established a consistent overall cognitive benefit.
Die Forschung zu Autophagie und Mitophag: Research on autophagy and mitophagy in humans is still at an early stage. An exploratory 2025 study found a between-group difference in one autophagy measure after six months of a substantially more intensive fasting programme, but no significant increase from baseline within the fasting group. This does not establish an autophagy effect from one weekly 18-hour fast. Mental clarity is not guaranteed either.

EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) and DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) are long-chain, polyunsaturated omega-3 fatty acids. They are components of cell membranes and are involved in various signaling and regulatory processes. DHA is found in particularly high concentrations in the brain and retina. While the plant-based omega-3 fatty acid ALA is found, for example, in linseeds, chia seeds and walnuts, fatty fish and certain microalgae in particular provide EPA and DHA directly. Algae oil is a plant-based source of EPA and/or DHA that is suitable for vegans. The quality of an oil depends, among other things, on the raw material, production, storage and oxidation stability. Products with transparent information on EPA and DHA quantities as well as traceable quality and purity tests make sense. A specific manufacturer cannot be generally classified as particularly recommendable without independent, current test data. People who don't eat fish can use algae oil as a direct source of EPA and DHA. Whether a supplement is necessary depends on the individual diet and supply. For healthy adults, there is no consistent recommendation that every person must take an EPA/DHA supplement. Regardless of this, the essential plant-based omega-3 fatty acid ALA should be consumed sufficiently through food. Omega-3 fatty acids can lower triglyceride levels. However, the study situation on the prevention of heart attacks, strokes or other cardiovascular events through over-the-counter supplements is differentiated: large studies and meta-analyses do not consistently show a relevant benefit for all healthy people. Certain high-dose prescription EPA preparations may have benefit in select individuals at high cardiovascular risk; These results cannot easily be applied to every dietary supplement. During pregnancy, DHA and other long-chain omega-3 fatty acids are relevant for the child's development. Studies show that adequate intake can reduce the risk of premature birth. However, the evidence for improving children's IQ through fish oil supplements is not clear. Pregnant women who do not eat fish should discuss their DHA or EPA supply with their healthcare professional. Further information:

Physical activity, a balanced diet, not smoking, adequate sleep and good management of chronic stress are examined in studies with various markers of health and cellular aging. Some research finds connections between a healthier lifestyle, telomerase activity and telomere length. However, the results are not uniform: the findings vary depending on the study design, the group of people examined and the measurement method. A systematic review of nutrition, for example, found evidence of connections between fruit and vegetable consumption or Mediterranean dietary patterns and longer telomeres. At the same time, the authors emphasize that many of the included studies were observational and further high-quality intervention studies are needed. Research on exercise also shows interesting results, but does not guarantee that a particular form of training will lengthen an individual's telomeres. Therefore, it makes sense to view exercise and a nutrient-rich diet as part of an overall health-promoting lifestyle - not as a targeted method to lengthen telomeres or halt aging.

Linoleic acid and arachidonic acid are involved in the formation of various messenger substances that can have both pro-inflammatory and inflammation-resolving or regulating functions. Telomeres are protective structures at the ends of our chromosomes. They consist of many repeats of a specific DNA sequence and proteins bound to it. Their job is to protect the chromosome ends from degradation and from the cell misrecognizing them as damaged DNA. With each cell division, telomeres can become shorter in many cell types. This is due, among other things, to the fact that DNA replication cannot completely copy the extreme ends of linear chromosomes. If telomeres reach a critical length or other cell stress signals arise, a cell can enter a state in which it no longer divides. Telomere length is therefore being investigated in research as a possible marker of cellular aging processes. However, it is not a sole or precise measure of a person's biological age: telomere length differs between people and cell types and is influenced by genetic, health and environmental factors.

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an essential nutrient. Among other things, it is needed for collagen formation, wound healing, normal immune system function and the absorption of non-heme iron from plant foods. It also acts as an antioxidant. Good sources include peppers, broccoli, brassicas, berries and citrus fruits. If you regularly eat enough fruit and vegetables, you can usually cover your vitamin C needs through your diet. Supplementation can make sense if the intake is permanently too low or there is an increased need or a medically justified risk. For example, people who smoke have a higher need for vitamin C than non-smokers. Higher doses are not automatically healthier. There is insufficient evidence to support the claim that high oral doses of vitamin C reliably prevent or treat cancer, cardiovascular disease or Alzheimer's disease. For colds, regular use can, on average, slightly shorten the duration of symptoms; However, in the general population it does not reliably prevent colds. Studies have shown that taking it after the cold has started has shown no consistent benefit. Very high amounts can cause gastrointestinal problems. In people with certain medical conditions, such as iron overload (hemochromatosis), high doses of vitamin C may pose additional risks. Therefore, taking high doses without a specific reason is not recommended. Unlike many other mammals, humans cannot produce vitamin C themselves and must obtain it through food. Vitamin D is important for calcium and phosphate metabolism and therefore for maintaining normal bones. It also contributes to normal muscle function. Unlike most vitamins, the body can produce vitamin D itself in the skin using UV-B radiation. In Germany, this formation is often severely restricted in winter due to the low position of the sun. However, this does not mean that every person automatically develops a vitamin D deficiency in winter or should take high doses of supplements. Care depends, among other things, on time spent outdoors, skin type, age, clothing, diet and other individual factors. For example, people who rarely spend time outdoors or rarely expose their skin to the sun have an increased risk of inadequate care. The German Society for Nutrition gives an estimated value of 20 micrograms (800 IU) of vitamin D per day if the body's own production is lacking. This value is not a general intake requirement for all people, but rather applies under the assumption that the skin does not produce vitamin D. Supplementation is particularly considered when an adequate supply cannot be achieved through the body's own education and nutrition. The intake of 60,000 IU per week for one month mentioned in the original text is not a general self-medication recommendation and should not be adopted across the board. High-dose treatments may be prescribed by a doctor in certain medical situations. Such high doses are unsuitable for independent, long-term use: an overdose can lead to increased calcium levels in the blood and other health problems. Zeolite and bentonite are mineral clays or aluminosilicates with special surface and binding properties. They can adsorb certain substances under laboratory conditions. However, it does not follow that they unspecifically remove “toxins”, mold or deposits in the human intestine and thereby restore the intestinal flora. There is no convincing clinical evidence to support routine use for detoxification or improving overall gut health. Depending on the product, purity and possible contamination can be an issue. Clay minerals can also bind to other substances in the digestive tract, potentially affecting the absorption of medications or nutrients. I therefore do not recommend self-treatment with zeolite or bentonite and especially no courses lasting several weeks without medical advice.
